defaults.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You stir a big spoonful of salt into a glass of water.
questions.question: What happens to the temperature at which the water freezes?
questions.explanation: To freeze, water molecules must lock into the orderly lattice of an ice crystal. Dissolved salt ions get in the way: they dilute the water and make it harder for molecules to join the crystal, so the mixture must get colder before it freezes. The effect depends on how many dissolved particles there are, not what they are, which is why sugar works too, just less strongly per spoonful.
questions.intuitionTrap: Adding 'stuff' to water feels like it should make it thicker and quicker to freeze.
questions.principle: Dissolved particles lower a solvent's freezing point (freezing-point depression).
questions.funFact: Seawater freezes at about −1.9 °C, and road salt stops being much use below roughly −10 °C.

questions.scenario: You put a sealed can of fizzy drink in the freezer to chill it quickly, then forget about it overnight.
questions.question: What's most likely to have happened by morning?
questions.explanation: At first, cooling actually lowers the pressure a little: cold liquid holds more dissolved CO₂ and cold gas pushes less. The trouble starts when it freezes. Water expands by about 9% as it turns to ice, and ice can't hold dissolved gas, so CO₂ is squeezed out of the freezing liquid into an ever-smaller space. The pressure climbs until the can bulges, the lid pops or a seam splits.
questions.intuitionTrap: Cold usually makes things contract, so freezing seems like it should shrink everything.
questions.principle: Water expands on freezing, and gases are expelled from growing ice crystals.
questions.funFact: The same expansion splits rocks: water seeping into cracks freezes, wedges them open and slowly breaks mountains apart.

questions.scenario: You grind a sugar cube into a very fine powder.
questions.question: Has it become a more reactive substance?
options: It reacts faster; its chemistry is unchanged
questions.reveal: It reacts faster, but its chemistry is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Grinding creates vastly more surface area, so anything that happens at the surface, such as dissolving or burning, goes much faster. Clouds of fine flour or sugar dust can even explode. But the molecules are identical: the same reactions are possible, they release the same energy per gram, and they reach the same equilibrium. Faster is not the same as more reactive.
questions.intuitionTrap: Seeing powder react violently suggests the substance itself has changed.
questions.principle: Surface area changes the rate of a reaction, not its thermodynamics.
questions.caveat: At the nanoscale, particles a few billionths of a metre across, surface atoms dominate and some materials do behave differently.
questions.funFact: Dust explosions are a real hazard in flour mills, grain silos and sugar refineries.

questions.scenario: A reaction A + B ⇌ C has settled into equilibrium in a sealed flask of solution. You inject extra A.
questions.question: Which way does the equilibrium shift?
options: Toward making more A and B
questions.explanation: Equilibrium isn't a frozen state: forward and reverse reactions keep running at equal rates. Adding A speeds up the forward reaction, because more A molecules are now colliding with B, so for a while C is made faster than it breaks down. The system shifts toward C until the two rates balance again, using up some of the A you added.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Equilibrium' sounds static, as if nothing is happening any more.
questions.principle: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium partly counteracts a change imposed on it.
questions.caveat: Adding more of a pure solid, such as extra limestone in CaCO₃ ⇌ CaO + CO₂, doesn't shift the equilibrium at all.
questions.funFact: Your blood uses this constantly: when you exercise and make extra CO₂, its carbonic-acid equilibrium shifts to buffer the change in acidity.

questions.scenario: You open a bottle of perfume in one corner of a closed room where the air feels still. A few minutes later, someone on the far side smells it.
questions.question: What mostly carried the smell across the room?
questions.explanation: Diffusion is real but painfully slow over long distances. Each molecule zig-zags randomly, colliding with air molecules billions of times a second, so the distance it spreads grows only with the square root of time. Crossing five metres by diffusion alone would take weeks. Even a 'still' room has slow drafts from warm bodies, lamps and windows, and those currents sweep the scent across in minutes.
questions.intuitionTrap: Textbooks use perfume as the classic diffusion example, so we credit diffusion for the whole trip.
questions.principle: Diffusion distance grows with the square root of time; over room-sized distances, convection dominates.
questions.funFact: Gas molecules at room temperature move at hundreds of metres per second; they just never get far before changing direction.

goDeeper.text: With a diffusion coefficient of about 0.07 cm²/s and L = 500 cm, t ≈ 1.8 million seconds: about three weeks.

questions.scenario: You sprinkle a handful of salt over a bowl of crushed ice and stir.
questions.question: What happens to the temperature of the icy mix?
questions.explanation: Salt lowers the freezing point, so the ice starts melting even though it's below 0 °C. Melting needs energy, and the quickest place to get it is from the mixture itself, so the temperature drops. A salt-and-ice mix can reach about −20 °C, which is how old-fashioned ice-cream makers freeze cream without a freezer.
questions.intuitionTrap: Salt 'melts ice' on roads, so it feels like it must be warming things up.
questions.principle: Melting absorbs latent heat; salt lets ice melt at lower temperatures and so pulls heat from the mix.
questions.funFact: The lowest temperature a salt-and-water mix can reach while staying liquid is about −21 °C.

questions.scenario: You take a strong acid at pH 2 and dilute it with water to ten times its original volume.
questions.question: What is its new pH?
questions.explanation: The pH scale is logarithmic: each step of 1 means a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion concentration. Diluting tenfold cuts the hydrogen ions to a tenth, so the pH rises by exactly one, from 2 to 3. The acid is still acidic; it would take another hundredfold dilution to reach pH 5.
questions.intuitionTrap: We expect a 'ten times' change to move a number by ten, or forget that pH goes up as acidity goes down.
questions.principle: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], so a tenfold dilution of a strong acid raises the pH by 1.
questions.caveat: No amount of dilution makes an acid basic: as it approaches neutral, water's own ions take over and the pH levels off near 7.
questions.funFact: Lemon juice (about pH 2) has around ten thousand times more hydrogen ions than black coffee (about pH 5–6).

questions.scenario: You pour vinegar onto baking soda in a cup. It fizzes wildly.
questions.question: Does the cup get warmer or colder?
questions.explanation: All that bubbling looks energetic, but this reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings: it's endothermic, so the mixture cools by a few degrees. What drives it forward isn't released heat but disorder. A solid and a liquid produce carbon dioxide gas that escapes, a big increase in entropy, and that is enough to make the reaction run even though it costs heat.
questions.intuitionTrap: Vigorous fizzing feels like an energetic, heat-releasing reaction.
questions.principle: Reactions can be driven by an increase in entropy even when they absorb heat.
questions.funFact: Instant cold packs work on a similar idea: dissolving ammonium nitrate in water absorbs heat and can chill the pack close to freezing.

questions.scenario: An iron nail is left outside until it has completely rusted. You carefully collect every flake of rust.
questions.question: How does the weight of the rust compare with the original nail?
questions.explanation: Rusting isn't iron crumbling away; it's iron combining with oxygen and water from the air. Those extra atoms add mass, so the rust (a hydrated iron oxide) weighs noticeably more than the iron did, roughly 40% more for plain iron oxide and more still with the water. Mass is still conserved overall: the extra came out of the air.
questions.intuitionTrap: Rust looks like decay, and decay feels like losing material.
questions.principle: In a chemical reaction mass is conserved; oxidation adds oxygen atoms to the metal.
questions.funFact: Antoine Lavoisier used careful weighing of metals heated in air to help overturn the 'phlogiston' theory of burning in the 1770s.

questions.scenario: Greasy hands won't come clean under running water, but a little soap gets the grease off easily.
questions.question: What does the soap actually do?
options: Grabs grease and water at once
questions.reveal: Its molecules grab grease with one end and water with the other.
questions.explanation: Water and oil don't mix, so water alone just slides over grease. A soap molecule has a long oil-loving tail and a water-loving head. The tails bury themselves in the grease while the heads stay in the water, and the grease breaks up into tiny droplets wrapped in soap, called micelles, which rinse away. The grease isn't destroyed, just escorted off.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Cleaning' sounds like the dirt is being chemically broken down.
questions.principle: Surfactants have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail, letting oil be carried away in water.
questions.funFact: Soap also destroys many viruses, including flu and coronaviruses, by tearing apart their fatty outer envelope.

questions.scenario: Gold is famous for being unreactive: it doesn't tarnish even after thousands of years. Now you divide gold into particles just a few nanometres across.
questions.question: Can those tiny gold particles act as a powerful chemical catalyst?
options: Yes, they can be very active
Only if the gold is molten
questions.reveal: Yes: nanoscale gold can be a highly active catalyst.
questions.explanation: In a particle only a few nanometres wide, a large share of atoms sit on surfaces, edges and corners, where their electrons behave differently from atoms buried inside bulk metal. In the 1980s, chemist Masatake Haruta showed that gold nanoparticles on a metal-oxide support can catalyse reactions such as turning carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide, even below room temperature. Bulk gold does nothing of the kind.
questions.intuitionTrap: We treat 'unreactive' as a fixed property of an element, whatever its size.
questions.principle: At the nanoscale, surface atoms dominate and properties can differ sharply from the bulk material.
questions.funFact: Gold nanoparticles aren't even gold-coloured: they look red or purple, and colour some medieval stained glass.

questions.scenario: People often say that energy is 'stored in chemical bonds' and released when fuel burns or ATP is used.
questions.question: When a chemical bond breaks, what happens to energy?
questions.reveal: Breaking a bond always absorbs energy.
questions.explanation: Pulling bonded atoms apart always takes energy. Energy is released when new bonds form. Burning fuel releases energy because the bonds in the products, carbon dioxide and water, are stronger than the bonds broken in the fuel and oxygen, so forming them gives back more energy than breaking the old ones cost. The energy is in the overall rearrangement, not in any single bond snapping.
questions.intuitionTrap: The phrase 'energy stored in bonds' suggests that breaking them sets the energy free.
questions.principle: Bond breaking is endothermic and bond forming is exothermic; a reaction's energy change is the difference.
questions.funFact: It's the same with magnets: separating two stuck magnets takes effort, and the energy comes out when they snap together.

questions.scenario: A cook chills an onion in the fridge for half an hour before chopping it, and cries much less.
questions.question: Why does the cold help?
options: Cold slows the reaction and evaporation
questions.reveal: Cold slows both the reaction and the evaporation.
questions.explanation: An intact onion contains no tear gas. Cutting breaks open cells and lets enzymes react with sulfur compounds, producing a volatile irritant that drifts up and stimulates nerves in your eyes. Like most reactions, these enzyme steps slow down in the cold, and the irritant evaporates more slowly too. Less of it reaches your eyes, so fewer tears.
questions.intuitionTrap: It seems like the chemical must be sitting in the onion already, waiting to escape.
questions.principle: Reaction and evaporation rates both drop as temperature falls.
questions.funFact: Researchers have bred 'tearless' onions with much lower levels of the compounds that start the reaction.

questions.scenario: A reversible reaction has reached equilibrium. You add a catalyst that speeds up the reaction.
questions.question: What happens to the amount of product?
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the energy barrier for the reaction, and the barrier is the same hill whichever way you cross it. So it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by exactly the same factor. It gets a reaction to equilibrium faster, but it cannot move where that equilibrium sits. If it could, you could build a perpetual-motion machine by adding and removing catalyst.
questions.intuitionTrap: If something speeds up a reaction, it feels like it should produce more of the product.
questions.principle: Catalysts change the rate of reaching equilibrium, never the equilibrium position.
questions.funFact: The catalysts in the Haber process that makes ammonia for fertiliser help feed billions of people, but they only speed it up; temperature and pressure decide the yield.

questions.scenario: You push a zinc-coated nail and a copper coin into a lemon, wire them up, and a tiny LED glows.
questions.question: Where does the electrical energy mainly come from?
questions.reveal: From the zinc being slowly eaten away.
questions.explanation: The lemon is mostly a convenient electrolyte, a salty, acidic liquid that lets ions move. The energy comes from the zinc: it gives up electrons and slowly dissolves (it is oxidised). Those electrons flow through the wire to the copper, where hydrogen ions from the juice pick them up. The copper isn't used up at all. Swap the lemon for a potato or salty water and it still works.
questions.intuitionTrap: The lemon is the star of the demo, so it gets the credit.
questions.principle: Batteries convert the chemical energy of a redox reaction into electrical energy.
questions.funFact: It takes several lemons wired in series to light even one small LED.

questions.scenario: The oceans have absorbed a large share of the CO₂ released by burning fossil fuels, a process called ocean acidification.
questions.question: Has seawater actually become acidic (pH below 7)?
questions.reveal: No; it's still basic, just less so.
questions.explanation: Surface seawater has a pH of about 8.1, which is basic. Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which nudges the pH downward: it has fallen by about 0.1 since pre-industrial times. Because the scale is logarithmic, that small number means about 25–30% more hydrogen ions. 'Acidification' describes the direction of change, not the destination, and even this shift makes it harder for corals and shellfish to build their shells.
questions.intuitionTrap: The word 'acidification' suggests the water has already become an acid.
questions.principle: pH is logarithmic, and 'acidifying' means moving toward lower pH, not crossing below 7.
questions.funFact: Some shellfish farms on the US Pacific coast have adjusted how they raise oyster larvae because of more corrosive seawater.
